meta.title: Spotting a phishing email
meta.description: In fifteen minutes, learn to spot the signs of a fraudulent email and respond without taking risks.
obj.signs: Identify the warning signs of a phishing email.
obj.react: Apply the right response to a suspicious email.
s1.title: Understanding the threat
s1.welcome.title: Welcome
s1.welcome.heading: One click is enough
s1.welcome.body: Phishing means posing as a trusted contact to obtain a password, a payment or the opening of a booby-trapped file. It is the entry point for **most cyberattacks**: attackers target people rather than machines.
s1.goals.heading: By the end of this module, you will be able to:
s2.title: Warning signs
s2.signals.title: Five signs to check
s2.signals.intro: A single sign proves nothing. Several signs together should stop you.
s2.signal.sender.title: An almost familiar sender
s2.signal.sender.body: The display name looks familiar, but the actual address is different: one changed letter, an unusual domain, a personal address for an "official" message.
s2.signal.urgency.title: Urgency or a threat
s2.signal.urgency.body: "Your account will be suspended in 24 hours." Time pressure is there to stop you from thinking.
s2.signal.links.title: Links that don't go where they say
s2.signal.links.body: Hover over a link (or long-press on mobile) to see its real destination before opening it.
s2.signal.attachments.title: An unexpected attachment
s2.signal.attachments.body: An unknown invoice, a document "to approve": an attachment you weren't expecting may contain malware.
s2.signal.requests.title: An unusual request
s2.signal.requests.body: No legitimate service asks for your password by email. A change of bank details must always be confirmed through another channel.
s2.example.title: A worked example
s2.example.heading: Three signs in a single message
s2.example.body:
Here is a message received on a Monday morning. Sender: "Payroll <payroll@hr-employee-portal.com>". Subject: "Action required: your payslip is on hold". Text: "Log in before 12 pm to avoid a payment delay."

**1. The address.** The name "Payroll" is reassuring, but the domain *hr-employee-portal.com* is not the company's.

**2. The urgency.** "Before 12 pm" and "payment delay" create pressure to act without checking.

**3. The request.** You are pushed to log in through a link, meaning you would type your password on an unknown page.

Taken one by one, each of these could have an explanation. Together, they should stop you.
s2.example.alt: Sign-in page opened by the link in the message: the address bar shows the domain payroll.secure-login.co, which does not belong to the company, above a username and password form.
s2.anatomy.title: Anatomy of a message
s2.anatomy.intro: Explore the four areas to check on this suspicious message.
s2.anatomy.alt: Mock-up of an email: the sender and their address, a subject marked with an alert and a clock, a button whose real address appears on hover, and a ZIP attachment.
s2.anatomy.sender.title: The sender's address
s2.anatomy.sender.body: The display name is reassuring, but the address is what counts: *hr-employee-portal.com* is not the company's domain.
s2.anatomy.subject.title: The subject
s2.anatomy.subject.body: An alert icon and a clock: urgency pushes you to act without checking.
s2.anatomy.link.title: The button
s2.anatomy.link.body: On hover, the real address appears: the domain is *secure-login.co*, unknown to your company.
s2.anatomy.attachment.title: The attachment
s2.anatomy.attachment.body: A ZIP archive you weren't expecting may contain malware.
s2.practice.title: Practice
s2.practice.prompt: You receive "IT Service <support@it-helpdesk-secure.net>: your mailbox is full, click here within 2 hours". Which signs do you spot?
s2.practice.a: The sender's address does not belong to your company.
s2.practice.a.fb: This is a sign: an internal service writes from the company domain. Reflex: always look at what follows the @.
s2.practice.b: The message is about your mailbox.
s2.practice.b.fb: This is not a sign in itself: genuine messages also talk about your mailbox. It's how the request is made (deadline, link) that should alert you.
s2.practice.c.fb: This is a sign: a very short deadline is meant to make you act before you think.
s2.where.prompt: On this page, which element really tells you which site you are on?
s2.where.alt: Sign-in page: an address bar with a padlock, a logo, a form and a button.
s2.where.padlock.fb: The padlock only means the connection is encrypted. A fake site can show it too.
s2.where.domain: The domain name in the address bar
s2.where.domain.fb: The domain, just before the first "/", identifies the real site: here, *secure-login.co*.
s2.where.logo.fb: A logo can be copied in one click: it says nothing about the site showing it.
s2.where.button.fb: A button looks the same on a real site and on a copy.
s3.title: Responding well
s3.react.title: Three reflexes
s3.react.intro: When in doubt, the right response is simple and risk-free.
s3.step.stop.title: Don't interact
s3.step.stop.body: Don't click any link, don't open any attachment and don't reply. If you're unsure about a real contact, reach them through a channel you already know.
s3.step.report.title: Report it
s3.step.report.body: Use your organization's report button or address. Your report also protects colleagues who received the same message.
s3.step.clicked.title: If you already clicked
s3.step.clicked.body: Don't panic, but act fast: alert IT support immediately and change the affected password from the official website. The sooner the alert, the smaller the damage.
s4.title: Assessment
s4.quiz.title: Check your knowledge
q.sender.prompt: The display name is "Finance Department", the address is finance@your-company-payment.com. What do you conclude?
q.sender.a: The message is trustworthy, since the name matches a real department.
q.sender.a.fb: Anyone can choose a display name; it proves nothing. Reflex: read the full address, then the domain after the @.
q.sender.b: It's suspicious: the domain looks like the company's but isn't the right one.
q.sender.b.fb: Adding a word to the company domain is a classic impersonation technique: the domain looks like the real one without being it.
q.sender.c: You can't conclude anything without opening the attachment.
q.sender.c.fb: Opening the attachment is precisely the risk to avoid. The address alone is already enough to raise doubt.
q.signals.prompt: An email asks you to "confirm your password" through a link. Which of the following are warning signs?
q.signals.a: The request for your password by email.
q.signals.a.fb: This is a sign: no legitimate service asks for your password by email.
q.signals.b: The link leads to an address different from the text shown.
q.signals.b.fb: This is a sign: it's the most common way to lead you to a fake site. Reflex: hover over the link before clicking.
q.signals.c: The message shows the company's official logo.
q.signals.c.fb: This is not a reliable sign either way: a logo can be copied in one click. Its presence doesn't prove the message is genuine.
q.signals.d: The message addresses you by your first name.
q.signals.d.fb: This is not a reliable sign: your first name is easy to find online. A personalized message is not necessarily a safe one.
q.link.prompt: A link's text reads "https://www.your-bank.com". When you hover over it, you see "http://your-bank.secure-login.co/signin". What do you conclude?
q.link.a: The link is safe, since the bank's name appears in it.
q.link.a.fb: The bank's name can appear anywhere in an address. What matters is the actual domain: here, *secure-login.co*.
q.link.b: The link is suspicious: the actual domain is not the bank's.
q.link.b.fb: The actual domain is read just before the first "/": *secure-login.co*, which does not belong to the bank.
q.link.c: The link is safe if it shows a padlock once opened.
q.link.c.fb: The padlock only means the connection is encrypted, not that the site is the right one. Fake sites often have one.
q.report.prompt: You receive a suspicious email that seems to have been sent to your whole department. What do you do?
q.report.a: I forward it to my colleagues to warn them.
q.report.a.fb: Forwarding the message spreads the booby-trapped link and makes it more credible. The alert should go through the reporting channel.
q.report.b: I report it using the button or address provided, without clicking.
q.report.b.fb: Reporting lets the security team block the message for everyone, in one go.
q.report.c: I reply to the sender to ask whether the message is legitimate.
q.report.c.fb: Replying confirms to the attacker that your address is active, and the attacker is the one who will answer.
q.verify.prompt: A regular supplier writes to you, from their usual address, that their bank details have changed. New bank details are attached. What do you do?
q.verify.a: I update the bank details: the sender's address is the right one.
q.verify.a.fb: A legitimate mailbox can be hacked. A correct address is not enough for a sensitive request such as a change of bank details.
q.verify.b: I reply to the email to ask for confirmation.
q.verify.b.fb: If the mailbox is hacked, the attacker is the one who will confirm. Verification must go through another channel.
q.verify.c: I call the supplier on the number I already know.
q.verify.c.fb: Checking through an independent channel (a number you already know, not the one in the message) is the only reliable way to confirm.
q.react.prompt: You clicked a suspicious link and entered your password. What do you do first?
q.react.a: I wait to see if anything unusual happens.
q.react.a.fb: Waiting gives the attacker time to use your password: every minute counts.
q.react.b: I delete the email to remove the traces.
q.react.b.fb: Deleting the email doesn't protect the account and deprives support of information useful for investigating.
q.react.c: I alert IT support and change my password from the official website.
q.react.c.fb: Alerting quickly and changing the password cuts off the attacker's access and limits the damage.
s4.recap.title: Summary
s4.recap.heading: Key takeaways
s4.recap.p1: Check the sender's actual address, not just the display name.
s4.recap.p2: Urgency, misleading link, unexpected attachment, unusual request: several signs together should stop you.
s4.recap.p3: When in doubt, don't click and report it. If you clicked, alert immediately.
s4.recap.p4: Before clicking, ask yourself three questions: was I expecting this message? Is the address the right one? Am I being pushed to act fast?
